findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so denials leak between anonymous and render subjects
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent. The identity type is not part of the key. `Check` reads the denial cache before it looks at `IdentityType`. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both have UID `0`, so they share a key. The existing permission cache avoids this by using a separate `anonymousPermCacheKey`. If anonymous is denied `dashboards:read` on dash1, a later `render:0` check for the same dashboard hits that entry and is wrongly denied, even though the renderer is granted read on everything. The reverse also happens: a render denial for a write action can deny an anonymous Editor. Include the identity type in the key, or use a separate prefix per type.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with '_' and names can contain '_'
findings.body: The key is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, and Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores. `name="a_b", parent="c"` and `name="a", parent="b_c"` produce the same key, so a denial for one resource denies the other for the whole TTL. The key also shares the `.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix with `userPermCacheKey`, so the two caches are only kept apart by their value types. Use a distinct prefix such as `perm_denial_` and a separator that cannot occur in the fields, or hash the parts.

findings.title: Every distinct denied resource now triggers a full DB permission re-query
findings.body: In `Check`, when the cached scope map does not allow the request, the code always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`. That runs `GetUserBasicRole`, `ListUserTeams` and `GetUserPermissions` against the DB, and `getUserPermissions` no longer short-circuits on the cache. The denial cache is keyed per (user, action, name, parent), so it only helps for repeats of the exact same resource. A user who is legitimately denied on many different dashboards or folders, for example a UI list of items or a scan, causes one DB permission query per distinct resource within each 30s window. Singleflight only merges concurrent calls. This removes most of the protection the permission cache gave and can amplify load on the DB. Consider rate-limiting the refresh per user/action, or negative-caching at the (user, action) level for a short time after a refresh.

findings.title: Denials computed from a possibly stale folder tree are cached with no invalidation
findings.body: After the DB re-query, `checkPermission` calls `checkInheritedPermissions`, which uses `buildFolderTree`. That tree is itself cached for 30s and is not refreshed by the permission re-query. For a newly created nested folder whose permission comes only from an ancestor, the stale tree does not contain the folder, so the check is denied. That result is then stored in the denial cache for another 30s, with no way to clear it when the folder tree or the user's permissions change. Access to newly created resources can stay denied for up to a minute even though the re-query was meant to fix exactly this case.

findings.title: Denial-cache test passes even if the denial cache is ignored
findings.body: The test comment says it allows access in `permCache` 'to prove this is not checked', but the cached map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, which also denies. Without the denial-cache lookup, `Check` would see a cached deny, fall back to the default `fakeStore` (no permissions), and still return `Allowed=false`. The test therefore cannot tell whether the denial short-circuit works. It should seed an allowing permission (`true`, or a store that grants access) and assert the store is not called. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed deny populates `permDenialCache`, and none that a later identical check skips the DB.
